$comment:
★★★ THE x86_64 AT&T ASSEMBLY DIALECT — a peer SOURCE LANGUAGE that reads a real `.s` file (plan 29 P2.5/P3/P4, 2026-08-12).

★★★ WHY A DIALECT IS A LANGUAGE AND NOT A `.target.json` KNOB. This is the operator's 2026-08-12 ruling, and it REVERSED a facet that had already been written, built and gated. An `asmSyntax` block carrying `registerPrefix`/`immediatePrefix`/`commentPrefixes`/operand order was added to both `.target.json` files; it loaded, it was fully config-driven, it had no identity branch, and the Windows leg was green with it in. It was wrong anyway. ✔MEASURED with gcc on ONE target: AT&T `movq %rsi, (%rdi)` versus Intel (`-masm=intel`) `mov QWORD PTR [rdi], rsi` — the same CPU and the same compiler, differing in register sigil, immediate sigil, comment character, OPERAND ORDER, memory-operand form AND mnemonic spelling. Per [[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]] both are legal `.s` input, so Intel is not optional forever ⇒ every one of those is a function of (target, DIALECT), and storing a per-(X,Y) fact per-X is the same duplication shape that killed the verbatim `_fstat$INODE64` binding. The decisive one is lexical rather than merely duplicative: `#` is a COMMENT here and the IMMEDIATE marker on arm64, so two dialects cannot share one `tokens` block even in principle.
⇒ `.target.json` keeps VOCABULARY ONLY (`opcodes[]`, `registers[]` — unchanged by this arc). This document owns the GRAMMAR, the token table, and the spelling→opcode map, and reaches the shared line structure in `asm.lang.json` through `languageReferences` — the same mechanism `c-subset.lang.json` uses to embed `__asm__(…)`. That reuse is the point: a third dialect writes a token table and ONE operand rule and inherits all seven line-structure rules.

★★ WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT KNOW: which registers exist, which opcodes exist, or how anything encodes. `%rax` resolves through `TargetSchema::registerByName`, `mov` through `TargetSchema::opcodeByMnemonic`, and an unresolvable name is a precise diagnostic naming the target — never a fallback. That is what keeps a dialect document from becoming a second, drifting copy of the target description.

⚠ THE INSTRUCTION TABLE'S LENGTH IS A VOCABULARY SIZE, NOT A MISSING MECHANISM. An undeclared mnemonic fails loud naming this dialect and the target, so growing it is a config edit with no code change. What is NOT vocabulary — a genuinely new operand SHAPE, a new addressing form — is grammar, and lands in `shapes` below.

language.$comment:
★ THE NAME CARRIES BOTH AXES (`asm` · `x86_64` · `att`) BECAUSE BOTH ARE REAL. `asm-x86_64-intel` is the sibling this shape exists to make cheap, and `asm-arm64-gas` is the other CPU. A name of just `asm` would have implied one assembly language, which is the assumption the operator's review disproved.
★ `.s` AND `.S` ARE BOTH CLAIMED. gas reads `.S` as 'run the C preprocessor first'; DSS does not preprocess assembly yet, so a `.S` carrying `#include` FAILS LOUD at parse rather than silently ignoring the directive. That is the honest state — claiming the extension and refusing the content beats not claiming it and giving 'no language for .S'.
⚠ TWO DIALECT DOCUMENTS CLAIMING `.s` IS AMBIGUOUS FOR EXTENSION-BASED ROUTING, AND THE AMBIGUITY IS REAL RATHER THAN A BUG IN THIS FILE: an assembly file is target-specific BY NATURE (no `.s` compiles for both x86_64 and arm64), so 'which dialect' is answered by the target, not by the extension. Until a driver reads that answer off the target, `--language asm-x86_64-att` names it explicitly — which is also what the examples corpus does. Anchored: D-DRIVER-ASM-DIALECT-SELECTED-BY-TARGET.
language.name: AsmX86_64Att

$isaComment: ★★★ THE ARCHITECTURE THIS LANGUAGE EMITS (D-ISA-LANGUAGE-BOUND-TO-ARCHITECTURE) — the LANGUAGE half of the axis whose TARGET half is `target.isa` in a `.target.json`. This document's surface IS the x86-64 instruction set, so it cannot be assembled for any other architecture — that is DEFINITIONAL, in the same sense that a document cannot be written in two languages at once, and nothing downstream could translate it. The gate (`crossValidateLanguageTarget`) refuses this language on any target whose `isa` differs, at the driver for a root build and at RESOLVE time for a `dependsOn` dependency. ★ ABSENT MEANS PORTABLE, AND ABSENT IS THE DEFAULT: `c-subset`, `toy`, `tsql-subset` and the shared `asm` core all declare NO `isa` and build for every target, paying nothing for this axis existing. Only a language that IS an instruction set declares one. ⚠ THIS IS NOT A LIST OF SUPPORTED PLATFORMS. A per-project target ENUMERATION was rejected (operator, 2026-08-14) because `targets[]` is a BUILD LIST that drifts, so reading it as a capability claim makes a portable project that merely forgot to list an arch refuse a legitimate consumer. An ISA binding cannot drift that way — a NEW target document declaring `isa: "x86_64"` satisfies THIS binding with no edit to this file. If anything ever requires editing this key because a target was added, the rejected design has been rebuilt. ⓘ Compared by EQUALITY only — no subset/superset lattice, because 'x86-64 code also runs in a 32-bit x86 process' is exactly the capability claim this axis refuses to make. The sibling `asm-x86_64-intel` this shape exists to make cheap would declare THE SAME value; the syntax axis and the ISA axis are independent, which is why the name carries both.

languageReferences.$comment:
★★ THE SHARED LINE STRUCTURE, REACHED BY REFERENCE. `entry: "asmLine"` imports exactly the rules reachable from it and NOTHING of the embedded `__asm__(…)` surface — the entry-closure scoping in `mergeLanguageReferences`. That scoping is also why this document binds a SUBSET of the holes `asm.lang.json` declares: a host owes the holes ITS entry's closure spells, and a `.s` file has no host expressions and no `__asm__` keyword to bind.
★ `symbolName` AND `operandSeparator` ARE SPELLED BY BOTH SURFACES, so they are bound here too — the same role names `c-subset.lang.json` binds to ITS Identifier and Comma. Same roles, different vocabularies, one grammar: the property the mechanism exists to have.

★★★ FIVE MORE BINDINGS ARRIVED 2026-08-15 WITH THE TEMPLATE PLACEHOLDER SURFACE (D-ASM-DIALECT-DECLARES-NO-OPERAND-PLACEHOLDER), and FOUR of the five name kinds this document declares ONLY inside its `asm-template` lexer mode. That is the whole trick and it is worth stating where a reader will look for it: the shared grammar's `%0` / `%[name]` / `%l[label]` shapes cannot be spelled with THIS document's `%`, because `%` is already `RegisterSigil` and `detectAmbiguousAlternatives` refuses two sibling alts sharing a FIRST token (EXERCISED, not read — two tests in `test_asm_shipped_dialects.cpp` watch the loader refuse the naive arm). Binding them to mode-only kinds makes the FIRST sets disjoint AND makes a placeholder unreachable from a `.s`, which is the behaviour gas has.
★ `templateOperandIndex` -> `IntLiteral` is the ONE of the five that is an ordinary global kind: a placeholder's index is the same integer literal `$8` already uses, and minting a second numeric kind for it would have been a distinction with no difference.
⚠ A per-mode-only kind IS bindable, and that is the loader's own contract rather than an accident: `bindTokens` resolves against the SchemaTokenInterner, and a per-mode `tokens` table is interned through the very same `parseMeaningArray` the global table uses. This document is the first shipped consumer of that property.

$tokensComment:
⚠ THIS BANNER SITS AT DOCUMENT LEVEL, NOT INSIDE `tokens`, AND THE LOADER IS RIGHT TO INSIST. A key in the `tokens` map is a LEXEME — arbitrary source text — not a name from a vocabulary the loader owns, and `$` is an ordinary operator character in real languages. There is deliberately no `$`-documentation carve-out there, so a `$comment` inside the map declares a token spelled `$comment`. ✔MEASURED: it failed loud as 'value must be an array of meaning objects' the first time this file was loaded.

★★★ THE NEWLINE IS NOT WHITESPACE, AND THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST LOAD-BEARING LINE IN THE FILE. Assembly is line-oriented: there is no statement terminator, so the newline IS the terminator. Every other shipped language flags `\n` as `EmptySpace` (the parser then never sees it); doing that here would not produce a parse error — it would produce a WRONG PARSE, with `ret` on one line swallowing the next line's `movq` as an operand. `LineEnd` therefore carries NO flags and is a first-class token the grammar names.
★ `\r` STAYS `EmptySpace` so a CRLF file behaves exactly like an LF one — the `\r` is skipped and the `\n` still terminates the line. A `\r\n` pair modelled as two significant tokens would make every Windows-authored `.s` a parse error, and a `\r` modelled as a line terminator would double every line.
★ `#` IS THE COMMENT INTRODUCER ON x86 gas, and it consumes to end-of-line EXCLUSIVE — the newline must survive as its own `LineEnd`, or a comment-terminated line would lose its terminator and merge with the next. This is verbatim the shape `c-subset.lang.json` uses for `//` (`$endsAtExclusiveComment` there), and the reason is the same one restated at a different tier.
⚠ `#` BEING A COMMENT HERE AND THE IMMEDIATE MARKER ON arm64 IS THE MEASUREMENT THAT MADE A DIALECT A LANGUAGE. It is not a stylistic difference that a shared table could parameterise: the same byte opens a comment in one dialect and a value in the other.
★ `@` IS THE SYMBOL-TYPE SIGIL, ADDED SO `.type main, @function` CAN LEX. It was undeclared until the `functionEntry` verb needed it, and the note that used to sit here ("the `@function` operand is not yet lexable, so a `.type` line currently fails at the tokenizer") described exactly that state. ⚠ IT IS NOT A GENERAL `@`: gas also writes `foo@PLT` and `foo@GOTPCREL`, which are symbol SUFFIXES with a different shape (no space, attached to a name, meaning a relocation kind) and are still UNDECLARED. Declaring the sigil does not declare those, and a `foo@PLT` operand now lexes but fails in the grammar rather than the tokenizer — a different, still-loud diagnostic.
⚠ STILL NO `;`, NO `=`: gas's statement separator and `.set`-style assignment are real gas syntax this dialect does not model. UNDECLARED rather than half-declared, so they fail loud at the tokenizer rather than parsing into something else. Anchored: D-ASM-ATT-GAS-SURFACE-INCOMPLETE.
⚠ AND ONE CONSEQUENCE OF THE `directiveIntroducer` CHOICE: a gas LOCAL label (`.L3:`) opens with the directive dot, so `asmElement` routes it to `asmDirective`. ⓘ UPDATED 2026-08-13 — the trailing `:` NO LONGER 'has nowhere to go': `asm.lang.json`'s `asmDirective` grew an `{optional asmLabelTail}` slot, so `.L3:` now PARSES in both dialects (✔MEASURED: `P0001 expected 'LineEnd' — got ':'` BEFORE, accepted AFTER, same binary and same input). What is still missing is the CONSUMER half — an `asmDirective` node carrying a label tail is a LABEL DEFINITION, not a directive, and the walker still routes it to the directive-vocabulary lookup, so `.L3:` fails loud as `A0008 unknown assembler directive '.L3'`. A dot-prefixed label is therefore PARSEABLE and not yet DEFINABLE, and the corpus still uses plain identifiers (`Lwin`, `Lfail`) for branch targets, which gas accepts identically. ✔MEASURED that this matters: every `-S` output of gcc uses `.L`-prefixed labels, so reading a compiler-emitted `.s` needs both halves. Anchored: D-ASM-DOT-PREFIXED-LOCAL-LABELS-UNPARSEABLE (grammar half done) and D-ASM-DOT-PREFIXED-LABEL-NOT-DEFINED-BY-CONSUMER (the other half).
⚠ AND A DOTTED NAME IS STILL NOT AN OPERAND: `jmp .L3` fails at the tokenizer/grammar seam (`P0001 expected 'LineEnd' — got '.'`) because no `attOperand` arm opens with `DirectiveDot`. Defining a `.L` label and BRANCHING to one are two separate gaps and only the first has moved.

★★★ `%%` IS A TOKEN OF THE TEMPLATE MODE, NOT OF THIS TABLE — MOVED 2026-08-15 (D-ASM-DIALECT-DECLARES-NO-OPERAND-PLACEHOLDER), AND THE MOVE IS THE CONFORMANCE HALF OF THE PLACEHOLDER WORK. It shipped HERE from 2026-08-14 to 2026-08-15 with no shape referencing it, which was the correct interim state while `.s` was the only surface. It stopped being correct the moment `attRegister` grew its `PercentEscape Identifier` arm: with the row global, that arm would make a standalone `.s` ACCEPT `%%eax`, and gas rejects it — accepting what no reference assembler accepts is a defect in the same direction as refusing what they do ([[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]] is bidirectional). ⇒ the row now lives in `lexerModes.asm-template.tokens`, where the arm is reachable from a TEMPLATE and unreachable from a `.s` BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by a check. Read that mode's banner for the measurements (extended "A%%0B" emits `A%0B`; the pair must never be unescaped and re-scanned) and for why the ordering mechanism is lexeme LENGTH rather than row order.
⚠ WHAT REMAINS TRUE OF **THIS** TABLE: `%` alone is the REGISTER SIGIL and nothing else, so a `.s` containing `%%eax` still fails LOUD — now with the two bytes read as two sigils rather than as one escape, which is the same refusal one token earlier.

lexerModes.$comment: The two comment bodies, verbatim in shape from `c-subset.lang.json`: every character inside becomes an `EmptySpace` CommentChar, and an unterminated body is reported as a comment rather than as a wall of stray tokens. The `endsAtExclusive` on `#` above is what keeps the terminating `LineEnd` outside the comment body — see the `tokens` banner.
lexerModes.$templateComment:
★★★ `asm-template` — THE SECOND LEXICAL SURFACE OF THIS DIALECT, AND THE ONLY ONE IN WHICH `%` IS NOT THE REGISTER SIGIL. ⚠⚠ IT IS EMPTY ON PURPOSE, AND THE EMPTINESS IS THE POINT (inline-asm P5c, 2026-08-17 — D-SEMANTIC-ASM-TEMPLATE-SIGILS-HARDCODED-BESIDE-A-CONFIG-OWNER, CLOSED). This mode used to declare five rows — `%%`, `%`, `%l`, `[`, `]` — and `scanInlineAsmTemplate` compared against the SAME bytes as C++ literals. Two owners of one fact, and NOTHING could detect them disagreeing: the semantic tier has no dialect in scope when it scans, so a dialect that declared a non-GNU sigil would lex one way and be scanned another, with a clean build log.
★★★ THE ROWS ARE NOW SYNTHESIZED BY THE LOADER, from `asm.lang.json`'s `semantics.inlineAsmTemplateLexemes` (the LANGUAGE's bytes) joined to this document's `bindTokens` (THIS dialect's kinds) by ROLE NAME. This document declares only the CAPABILITY — `assembly.templateLexerMode` naming this mode, plus `templateOperandRule` — and re-declaring any template lexeme here is a LOAD ERROR naming both sites, in both directions: the same BYTES, or the same role-bound KIND under different bytes (so 'spell it `@` instead' is refused as firmly as re-declaring `%`).
★ WHAT THE MODE STILL IS: not a body mode (no `defaultToken`), so the scanner runs its ordinary lexeme match and consults the synthesized table FIRST with the global table as fallback (`longestMatchInMode`). Entered ONLY by the template parse entry, which reads the mode's name from `assembly.templateLexerMode` — never from a hard-coded string — and never while reading a `.s`.

★★★ WHY A MODE AND NOT FIVE MORE GLOBAL ROWS — unchanged, and the measurement is what fixes it here. ✔MEASURED on gcc 13.3.0 and clang 18.1.3, sources fed as base64 so no shell could alter a byte: `__asm__("xorl %eax,%eax")` — BASIC — assembles, `%` is LITERAL; `__asm__("xorl %eax,%eax" ::: "eax")` — EXTENDED, and ANY colon makes it extended — is REJECTED by BOTH ("operand number missing after %-letter" / "invalid % escape in inline assembly string"); `__asm__("xorl %%eax,%%eax" ::: "eax")` assembles and emits `xorl %eax,%eax`. So the `.s` surface and the extended-template surface genuinely differ IN THE LEXER, not merely in what the parser accepts.
★★ WHAT EACH SYNTHESIZED ROW BUYS, AND WHICH `bindTokens` ROLE CARRIES IT.
  • `templateEscape` -> `PercentEscape` (`%%`) — the literal percent, and the ONLY way to write a register in an extended template (`%%eax`). ⚠ IT IS NOT IN THE GLOBAL TABLE, and that placement is the bidirectional-conformance half: `attRegister` has an arm reading `PercentEscape Identifier`, and with the lexeme global that arm would make a standalone `.s` ACCEPT `%%eax` — which gas rejects, and accepting what no reference accepts is a defect in the same way refusing what they accept is. Synthesized INTO this mode, the arm is unreachable from a `.s` BY CONSTRUCTION. ⓘ It is also the ONE role no shared SHAPE spells — see `asm.lang.json`'s `$templateEscapeHoleComment`.
  • `templatePlaceholder` -> `PlaceholderSigil` (`%`) — the operand placeholder. The second kind `%` needs, and the reason the mode exists at all.
  • `templateLabelPlaceholder` -> `PlaceholderLabelSigil` (`%l`) — the `asm goto` label sigil, TWO BYTES so maximal munch settles `%l[done]` versus `%0`. ⚠ It cannot shadow a mnemonic: the lexeme starts at the percent, so `lsl`/`leaq`/`ljmp` are untouched.
⚠⚠ THE `%l` ROW IS THE GRAMMAR HALF ONLY — NOTHING LOWERS A LABEL PLACEHOLDER. It makes `%l[done]` LEX and PARSE; the lowering then refuses it by name, because a label target must resolve to a BLOCK of the function that embedded the template and an operand binding carries a register and no block. See `asm.lang.json`'s `asmTemplateLabelRef`.
  • `symbolicNameOpen`/`symbolicNameClose` -> `PlaceholderNameOpen`/`PlaceholderNameClose` (`[`/`]`) — x86 AT&T gas has NO bracket of its own (memory is `-8(%rbp)`), so these two bytes are undeclared globally and stay that way: in a `.s` a `[` is still an 'unexpected character' at the TOKENIZER, the loudest place it can fail.

★★ THE MECHANISM THAT ORDERS `%%` AHEAD OF `%` IS LEXEME **LENGTH**, NOT DECLARATION ORDER — ✔MEASURED in `tokenizer.cpp`'s `longestMatchInMode`, which probes DOWN from the longest key; `nlohmann::json` sorts object keys anyway, so file order does not survive the parse. ⇒ a 'red on reordering' pin cannot exist. The pin that CAN exist now nulls the ROLE in `asm.lang.json` and watches this dialect's row disappear with it — which proves the derivation is LIVE, where the old row-deletion pin only proved two copies happened to agree.

⚠ NOTHING UNESCAPES. ✔MEASURED: extended `"A%%0B"` emits `A%0B` on gcc and clang and the `%0` that appears is NOT re-read as operand 0. Because `%%` is a lexeme of this mode, `%%0` lexes as PercentEscape + IntLiteral and no shape accepts it — refused loud, which is what the reference toolchain does one stage later when gas sees the emitted `%0`.

numberStyle.$comment: gas integer literals: decimal, `0x` hex, and a leading `0` octal. No float literals — a floating-point CONSTANT in a `.s` appears only inside a `.double`/`.float` directive, which this dialect does not model yet (an undeclared directive fails loud). Declaring float syntax we cannot lower would be the accept-and-ignore this project refuses.

shapes.$comment: ★ ONLY THE ROOT AND THE OPERAND PRODUCTION LIVE HERE. Everything between them — the line, the label chain, the directive, the statement, the operand sequence — arrives from `asm.lang.json`. That split is the reuse claim, and it is measurable: a new dialect's `shapes` block is this size, not the size of an assembly grammar.

root.$comment:
A `.s` translation unit: a run of lines, each terminated.
★★ THE FINAL NEWLINE IS MANDATORY, AND THAT IS A MEASURED DECISION RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. The first draft was `{repeat asmLine}` + a trailing `{optional asmElement}` to accept a file whose last line has no newline. ✔MEASURED: the loader REFUSED it — `C_AmbiguousAlternatives at /shapes/root: alt branches share FIRST token 'Identifier'` — and the refusal is right. After any complete line, an `Identifier` could open either another `asmLine` (which requires a terminator) or the unterminated final element, and LL(1) cannot tell them apart; the parser 'would silently take the first branch'.
★ THE ALTERNATIVES AND WHY EACH LOSES. Marking the terminator `{optional}` inside `asmLine` removes the ambiguity by removing the LINE DISCIPLINE — `ret` followed on the next token by `movq` would then parse as `ret movq` (an instruction with an operand), which is the exact wrong-parse the significant newline exists to prevent. `speculative: true` would work and would put backtracking into the one grammar in this tree that has none. Appending a newline to the buffer would be the driver rewriting the user's source.
⇒ A file whose last line lacks a newline is a LOUD parse error at that line. POSIX defines a line as ending in a newline and every toolchain that emits a `.s` writes one, so the cost is a precise diagnostic on a malformed file — against a silent misparse on a well-formed one. Anchored: D-ASM-FINAL-NEWLINE-REQUIRED.

attOperand.$comment:
★★ ONE AT&T OPERAND — five FIRST-disjoint forms, no speculation:
  • `%rax`            register        → RegisterSigil
  • `$42` / `$foo`    immediate       → ImmediateSigil
  • `(%rax,%rbx,8)`   memory, no disp → ParenOpen
  • `-8(%rbp)` `foo`  displaced memory OR a bare symbol → IntLiteral | Identifier | MinusSign
  • `*%rax`           indirect target → IndirectStar
  • `@function`       symbol-type marker → TypeSigil
★★ THE FOURTH ARM IS WHY `attDisplaced` EXISTS RATHER THAN SEPARATE `memory` AND `symbol` RULES: `foo(%rip)` and `foo` both open with an Identifier, so a two-arm alt would not be FIRST-disjoint. Reading the displacement first and making the base `{optional}` decides it on the following token — the same 'read once, dispatch on what follows' shape `asmStatement` uses for label-vs-mnemonic, and for the same reason.

attSectionName.$comment:
★★★ `.rodata` IN OPERAND POSITION — the shape `.section .rodata` needs (D-ASM-SECTION-DIRECTIVE-WITH-OPERAND-UNMODELLED, closed 2026-08-13). ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 with x86_64 `as`: `.section .rodata` assembles rc=0 into a `.rodata` PROGBITS+A section, a bare `.rodata` is `Error: unknown pseudo-op`, and — the part that makes the dot load-bearing — `.section rodata` WITHOUT the dot creates a section literally named `rodata` with NO allocation flag, i.e. a DIFFERENT section. So the introducer is part of the name and the consumer checks for it (read off the tree, never hardcoded).
★ NOT BOUND TO AN `operandForms` ROLE, exactly like `attTypeMarker` above and for the same reason: it is read as TEXT by the directive handler and resolved against this dialect's own section-opening directive ROWS, so an unroled rule reaching instruction position fails loud in `decodeOperand` — the right answer for `addq .rodata, %rax`.
★ IT MUST PRECEDE `attDisplaced` IN THE ALT only for readability; the two are FIRST-disjoint (`DirectiveDot` versus `IntLiteral | Identifier | MinusSign`), as is every other arm, so no speculation is introduced.
ⓘ THIS RULE ALSO REMOVES ONE HALF OF THE `jmp .L3` GAP the token banner records — a dotted name can now BE an operand. The other half (a dot-label as a BRANCH TARGET rather than a section name) is a `sectionByName`-independent question and is still open; nothing here claims it.

attTypeMarker.$comment:
`@function` / `@object` — the ELF symbol-TYPE marker, and the only operand form here that never appears on an INSTRUCTION. It exists so `.type main, @function` parses, and it is deliberately NOT bound to an `operandForms` role: a role is what an instruction operand is lowered THROUGH, and this one is read as TEXT by the directive handler (`AsmDirectiveSpelling::marker`) and compared against the dialect's declared marker string. An unroled rule reaching instruction position would fail loud in `decodeOperand` — 'operand shape is not one this dialect binds to an operand role' — which is the correct answer for `addq @function, %rax`.
★ THE MARKER TEXT IS DIALECT DATA, NOT ENGINE DATA, AND THE TWO SHIPPED DIALECTS PROVE WHY: ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13, gcc 13 on x86_64 emits `.type main, @function` while aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc emits `.type main, %function` — the same directive, the same meaning, a different sigil, because `@` is a comment character on 32-bit ARM and the ARM gas port never took it back. An engine that hard-coded `@function` would have rejected every aarch64 compiler output.

attRegister.$comment:
`%` + a bare name. The NAME is not vocabulary here — it resolves through the active `.target.json`'s `registers[]`, so `%rax` on a target that declares no `rax` is a precise diagnostic rather than a grammar error. A register list in this file would be exactly the target identity leak the bar forbids.

★★★ THE SECOND ARM IS `%%rax`, AND IT IS THE ONLY WAY TO NAME A REGISTER IN AN EXTENDED TEMPLATE (2026-08-15, D-ASM-DIALECT-DECLARES-NO-OPERAND-PLACEHOLDER). ✔MEASURED on gcc 13.3.0 and clang 18.1.3, sources fed as base64: `__asm__("xorl %eax,%eax" ::: "eax")` is REJECTED BY BOTH ("operand number missing after %-letter" / "invalid % escape in inline assembly string") while `__asm__("xorl %%eax,%%eax" ::: "eax")` assembles and emits `xorl %eax,%eax`. In an extended template `%`+letter is a MODIFIER, so the register sigil has to be doubled — and until this arm existed the literal-percent form had NO SPELLING AT ALL in this dialect, which is precisely what the anchor was opened for.

★★ IT IS AN INLINE `{sequence}` ARM RATHER THAN A NAMED SIBLING RULE, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN TERSE. A named rule MINTS A CST NODE, and the engine's register decode reads 'the last visible TOKEN child of the register node' — with a named inner rule the register node's children would be one INTERNAL node and no tokens at all, and every register in the dialect would decode as the empty spelling. Inline arms keep the two token children exactly where the decode already looks, for both arms, with no engine change.
★ FIRST-DISJOINT BY KIND: `RegisterSigil` versus `PercentEscape`, and `PercentEscape` is declared ONLY in the `asm-template` lexer mode — so a standalone `.s` can never take the second arm, which is what keeps this from accepting `%%eax` in a file gas would reject.

attImmediate.$comment: `$` + a scalar. gas also accepts a full constant EXPRESSION here (`$(1<<3)`); this dialect models a single scalar and fails loud on anything else, rather than accepting an expression it would then have to fold with semantics nobody declared.

attScalar.$comment: A displacement / immediate value: a number, a negated number, or a symbol name.

attNegNumber.$comment: `-8` — the ordinary frame-relative displacement. A separate rule (rather than a signed literal in `numberStyle`) because the sign is grammar: `-` is also a binary operator in gas expressions, and a signed-literal token would make `8-4` lex as two numbers.

attMemory.$comment: `(base)` / `(base,index)` / `(base,index,scale)` with NO displacement. The comma inside the parens can never be confused with the operand-list separator: the choice at this position is between `OperandComma` (an index follows) and `ParenClose` (the operand ends), which are distinct kinds, and the operand list's own `{repeat}` only resumes after this rule completes.

attDisplaced.$comment: A scalar, optionally followed by a memory base — `foo`, `-8(%rbp)`, `foo(%rip)`, `8(%rax,%rbx,4)`. Absent base ⇒ a bare symbol/absolute operand; present base ⇒ a displaced memory reference. The consumer distinguishes them by whether the `attMemory` child is there, a RuleId question.

attIndirect.$comment: `*%rax` / `*(%rax)` — gas's marker for an INDIRECT branch or call target. It is syntax, not decoration: `jmp foo` and `jmp *%rax` are different instructions, and dropping the star would silently turn an indirect jump into a direct one — a miscompile with no diagnostic. Modelled so the consumer can select the indirect opcode by RuleId.

pipelineEntry.$comment:
★★★ A `.s` TRANSLATION UNIT ENTERS AT THE ASSEMBLER'S INPUT. `encode` is the fourth tier (operator decision, plan 29 §5) and means post-regalloc, post-two-address-legalize, post-calling-convention. ✔MEASURED in `src/program/compile_pipeline.cpp`, a `.s` must enter after THREE passes and not one: `allocateRegisters` (:956) would reassign the programmer's registers, `legalizeTwoAddress` (:971) would rewrite the instruction forms, and `materializeCallingConvention` (:1008) would inject a prologue/epilogue OVER the one the programmer wrote. Entering at `lir` — which an earlier comment in `pipeline_entry_config.hpp` would have led an implementer to do — silently reframes every hand-written function.
★ AND THERE IS NO `optimize: false` SIBLING: entering at `encode` means no MIR module exists, so MIR passes cannot run BY CONSTRUCTION. 'Hand-written assembly is not optimized' is a consequence of the tier, never a second switch that could drift from it.

assembly.$comment:
★★★ THE TEXT→LIR CONTRACT: the rule landmarks the lowering reads, the ONE dialect-wide operand-order fact, and the spelling vocabulary. Everything here is a NAME the engine resolves — no behaviour, no branch.

★★★ `operandOrder` IS DECLARED ONCE, AND THE HISTORY OF THAT IS WORTH KEEPING. The reverted `asmSyntax` facet declared a `destinationOperand` PER INSTRUCTION, justified in three places by the claim *"that flag is already false for x86 store forms"*. ✔MEASURED: **false.** AT&T is uniformly destination-LAST *including stores* (`movq %rsi, (%rdi)`); Intel is uniformly destination-FIRST (`mov QWORD PTR [rdi], rsi`). Both dialects are internally uniform, so operand order is EXACTLY ONE dialect fact — and the per-instruction shape would have meant N edits to express the one thing that distinguishes Intel from AT&T. The claim was asserted without a probe and it invented the requirement it was used to satisfy.

★★ WHAT IS *NOT* DECLARED HERE, ON PURPOSE: which asm operand becomes the LIR RESULT versus a LIR OPERAND. That is derivable from facts the TARGET already states — `opcodes[].result` (`value` / `none`) and `opcodes[].requires2Address` — and re-declaring it per instruction would be a second source of truth for something `.target.json` owns. The derivation is: the destination operand (per `operandOrder`) becomes the LIR result when the opcode produces a value; the remaining operands follow in source order; a `requires2Address` opcode additionally takes the destination as its FIRST input, which is precisely the legalized form AT&T already writes. ⚠ An opcode whose shape does not fit that derivation FAILS LOUD naming the mnemonic — it is never fitted by guessing.

★ `instructions[]` maps an ASSEMBLY SPELLING to TARGET OPCODE NAMES plus the operand WIDTH the suffix encodes (`movq`→64, `movl`→32). ✔MEASURED and this is why the table exists at all: `opcodes[].mnemonic` is NOT assembly — the 86 x86_64 entries are DSS's virtual-ISA names (`shr_l`, `jcc`, `xor_rdx_zero`, `store_outgoing_arg`), while a real `.s` writes `movq`/`shrq`/`je`. A few overlap by coincidence (`mov`, `add`, `ret`), which is exactly what would have made reusing them LOOK like it worked.

★★★ `opcodes` IS AN ARRAY BECAUSE ONE AT&T SPELLING IS GENUINELY SEVERAL DSS OPCODES, AND `movq` IS THE PROOF: `movq %rcx, %rax` is `mov`, `movq (%rdi), %rax` is `load`, and `movq %rax, (%rdi)` is `store` — three opcodes, one mnemonic, distinguished ONLY by which operand is a memory reference. The walker elects among the listed names using the TARGET's own `encoding.variants[].guard.operandKinds`, so the dialect never decides which one; it only says which are POSSIBLE. `jmp` is the second case (`jmp foo` → `jmp`, `jmp *%rax` → `jmp_indirect`), and `call` the third.
⚠ A SINGLETON ARRAY IS NOT A WASTED FACILITY, IT IS A MEASUREMENT: `asm-arm64-gas.lang.json`'s rows are almost all singletons because arm64 does NOT overload — it spells load/store/move as `ldr`/`str`/`mov`. So WHICH spellings are overloaded is a DIALECT property, which is an independent argument for this array living in the dialect document rather than in the target.
⚠ AND THE ELECTION HAS TO SETTLE OPERAND PLACEMENT, NOT JUST OPCODE IDENTITY — ✔MEASURED against the two `result: none` opcodes this table now reaches, which DISAGREE under one positional rule. `cmpq $93, %rax` must become LIR `[rax, imm 93]` (written order REVERSED — LIR's `cmp` takes the LHS first, and AT&T writes the LHS last), while `movq %rax, 16(%rsp)` must become LIR `[rax, rsp, MemBase, MemOffset]` (written order PRESERVED — LIR's `store` takes the stored VALUE first). Both are `destinationLast`, both produce no value, and no rule phrased in terms of position alone gets both right. ⇒ placement is matched by KIND against the elected variant's `operandKinds`, which is also what keeps `lir_verifier`'s independent 'MemBase then MemOffset must be the last two operands' rule satisfied by construction.

★ `cond` NAMES AN EXISTING `TargetCondCode` — no new vocabulary was minted for the conditional branches. It is REQUIRED on a row whose elected target opcode declares `condCodeFromPayload` and REJECTED on one that does not, so a stray `cond` is a refusal rather than a silently-ignored key, and a missing one is a refusal rather than a silent encode of the target's zero condition.
★★ THAT KEY USED TO BE `terminatorKind == cond-br`, AND IT WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — fixed 2026-08-13, closing D-ASM-COND-ALLOWED-ONLY-ON-JCC. Both shipped targets declare exactly two condition-reading opcodes: `jcc` (a cond-br) and `setcc` (`terminatorKind: None`, `result: value`). Keyed on the terminator shape the rule coincided with the right answer on `jcc` and REFUSED a condition on `setcc` — the opcode whose only job is to materialize one. The encoder is the thing that actually decides, so the encoder's own declaration is now the key.
⚠ AND `sete`/`setne` ROWS ARE STILL NOT SHIPPED HERE, FOR A REASON THAT IS NOT THIS ONE. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13: gas writes `sete %al` — an 8-bit destination — and `x86_64.target.json` declares 49 registers with NO 8-bit file (16 GPR64, 16 GPR32, 16 xmm, rflags), so `%al` cannot resolve. The only destination this dialect could spell is `%rax`, which gas REJECTS, and shipping a row that accepts input no reference assembler takes is the same defect as refusing input they do accept ([[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]], which is bidirectional). The engine mechanism is landed and pinned through the ENCODED BYTE in tests/asm/test_asm_text_to_lir.cpp (`SetccCarriesItsConditionThroughToTheEncodedByte`); the rows land with the 8-bit register file. Anchored: D-ASM-X86-NO-8BIT-REGISTER-FILE.
assembly.$templateSurfaceComment:
★★★ THE THREE KEYS THAT MAKE AN EMBEDDED `__asm__` TEMPLATE READABLE BY THIS DIALECT (2026-08-15, D-ASM-DIALECT-DECLARES-NO-OPERAND-PLACEHOLDER; third key added P20). They are OPTIONAL AS A SET and REQUIRED OF EACH OTHER — the loader refuses any proper subset, because a mode with no rule mints placeholder tokens no shape accepts, a rule with no mode declares a shape whose FIRST token nothing ever produces, and a surface with no LABEL rule cannot tell an `asm goto` target from an operand. Every one of those is a silent no-op, which is the failure class this document's every other key is shaped to avoid.
★ `templateLexerMode` names the mode the TEMPLATE PARSE ENTRY starts in; `templateOperandRule` names the shared grammar's placeholder rule so the lowering engine can recognise a placeholder WITHOUT a hard-coded rule name; `templateLabelRule` names the LABEL alternative of that rule, which is how the engine asks `resolveBranchTarget` instead of `resolveRegister` without ever testing the `%l` bytes in C++.
⚠⚠ AND THE SET IS NOW MANDATORY FOR THIS DOCUMENT RATHER THAN OPTIONAL — a consequence of `D-CONFIG-ASM-TEMPLATE-CAPABILITY-NO-LONGER-OPTIONAL-FOR-A-SHARED-SURFACE-IMPORTER`, not a new policy: `asm.lang.json`'s `asmLine` closure SPELLS the template holes, so importing the shared standalone surface imports the placeholder shapes whether or not this dialect wants them. A dialect importing a NARROWER entry may still declare none of the three. The argument lives once, in `assembly_config.hpp`'s `templateLabelRule` docblock.
assembly.$spellingCaseComment:
★★★ gas IS CASE-INSENSITIVE ON EVERY SPELLING IT DECLARES, AND DSS WAS NOT — D-ASM-DIALECT-MNEMONIC-MATCH-IS-CASE-SENSITIVE. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-15, `as` (GNU Binutils for Ubuntu) 2.42, rc plus the encoded bytes read back with `objdump -d`: `movq %rax,%rcx`, `MOVQ %rax,%rcx` and `MoVq %rax,%rcx` all assemble to `48 89 c1`; `movq %RAX,%RCX` is the same three bytes and `movl %EAX,%ECX` is `89 c1`; `.TEXT`, `.GLOBL`, `.TYPE`, `.SECTION`, `.QUAD`, `.DATA`, `.BSS` and `.ZERO` are all rc=0. Refusing what the reference assembler accepts is a defect under [[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]], so this dialect folds — and it folds ALL FOUR surfaces (mnemonic, register, operand selector, directive) or none, because a half-fold just moves `MOVQ %RAX, %RCX`'s refusal one token to the right.

⛔ WHAT THIS KEY DOES **NOT** REACH, MEASURED IN THE SAME RUN AND AGAINST THE SAME ASSEMBLER — three surfaces where gas is case-SENSITIVE, and folding any of them would be a silent miscompile rather than a conformance fix: (1) SYMBOL/LABEL names — `foo:` and `FOO:` both appear in `nm` as two defined symbols, and `jmp FOO` against `foo:` leaves `FOO` `*UND*`; (2) the `.type` MARKER — `.type main, @FUNCTION` and `.type main, @Function` are BOTH rc=1 *"unrecognized symbol type"*, even though `.TYPE` itself is accepted, so the directive folds and its marker operand does not in one line; (3) the `.section` NAME operand — `.section .RODATA` is rc=0 and opens a section literally CALLED `.RODATA`, and a file writing both `.rodata` and `.RODATA` gets two 8-byte sections in `objdump -h`. The engine keeps all three exact.

operandForms.$comment: Which of THIS document's rules realizes each operand ROLE the lowering understands. The engine walks roles, never rule names, so a dialect whose memory form is `[base, #off]` binds the same five roles to different rules and needs no engine change.

instructions.$comment: ★★ THE OVERLOADED ROW. `movq` is `mov`, `load` OR `store` depending on where the memory operand sits, and the target's variant guards make the call — see the block banner. Order inside the array is NOT a priority list: the guards are mutually exclusive by operand kind, so an input matching two of them would be a target defect rather than something this ordering papers over.

★ EVERY `mov` ROW NAMES `mov_mem` FROM 2026-08-23 (cycle P29): `movq $5, -16(%rbp)` writes an IMMEDIATE into memory, and `store` takes a REGISTER source only — so before that opcode existed every such spelling was refused fail-loud with `no candidate target opcode encodes that shape`, at all four widths. The width-16 form is the one that needed [[D-ASM-X86-NO-16BIT-IMMEDIATE-SLOT]]: `movw $42, mem` is `66 C7 /0 iw`, a TWO-byte immediate the x86-variable walker had no slot for.

★★★ THE SUB-NATIVE MOVES (D-ASM-SUB-NATIVE-OPERAND-UNUSABLE-IN-INLINE-ASM, 2026-08-23). Without these two rows a `char` or `short` operand could not be used in ANY extended-asm template on this target: the substituted register width comes from the operand's own type, so `movl %1, %0` on a `char` is refused (`'movl' declares operand width 32, but its register operands are 8 bits`) and `movb` was not a spelling this table knew. gcc 13.3.0 compiles AND RUNS both programs (exit 42), which by bar §A.3b makes them REQUIRED.
★★ THE MEMORY-SOURCE OPCODE IS `load_subreg`, NOT `load`, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS A SILENT MISCOMPILE: the target's width-8/width-16 `load` rows are MOVZX (`0F B6` / `0F B7`), which ZERO the destination's upper bits — gas spells those `movzbl`/`movzwl`. AT&T `movb (%rax), %cl` is `8A /r`, which leaves them UNCHANGED. Naming `load` here would have encoded a different instruction than the source wrote, with no diagnostic anywhere.
⚠⚠ THIS PARAGRAPH SAID `movw $imm, %reg` IS STILL REFUSED AND IT WAS FALSE IN ITS OWN COMMIT — corrected 2026-08-24 by the independent step-10 audit, which is the whole reason to record it rather than quietly delete it. The clause was written while [[D-ASM-X86-NO-16BIT-IMMEDIATE-SLOT]] was still open; the SAME commit closed it, so `EncodingSlotKind::Imm16Bytes` exists, `mov` carries the width-16 `66 C7 /0 iw` variant that uses it, and ✔MEASURED at the CLI an inline-asm `movw` of an immediate into an `"=r"` short on `x86_64:pe64-x86_64-windows-exec` builds rc=0 and the artifact RUNS returning 42. ★ The species is worth naming because a guard cannot see it: a comment that was true when the sentence was typed and false when the commit landed still READS as evidence, and this one would have sent the next author to fix an engine gap that no longer exists. `movb $imm, %reg` also works — `C6 /0 ib` rides the 1-byte slot.

★★★ THE ARITHMETIC ROWS NAME **TWO** OPCODES EACH FROM 2026-08-23 (D-TARGET-X86-64-DECLARES-NO-MEMORY-DESTINATION-ARITHMETIC), and it is the same overloading `movq` has had all along: `addq $5, %rax` is `add`, `addq $5, -16(%rbp)` is `add_mem`, and which one an input denotes is decided by the TARGET's variant guards plus the engine's producer/consumer split — never by this table. ✔MEASURED, GNU as 2.42: `add`, `sub`, `and`, `or`, `xor` and `cmp` all take a memory destination with an immediate OR a register source; `imul` takes NONE (its two-operand form writes a register), and `lea`'s destination is a register by definition — which is why those two rows stay singletons. The memory-SOURCE direction needs no second name: it is a variant on the producer opcode already listed.
⚠ `cmpq`/`cmpl` STAY SINGLETONS FOR A DIFFERENT REASON, AND IT IS A REAL GAP RATHER THAN AN ABSENCE OF DEMAND: `cmp` is `result: none`, so its row lists no producer, so the engine offers BOTH the memory-destination and the memory-source operand lists to the same candidate set — and those two lists are byte-identical while denoting opposite operand orders. Declaring either would silently encode the other for the opposite spelling. Anchored: [[D-ASM-X86-CMP-AGAINST-MEMORY-DIRECTION-IS-UNELECTABLE]].

★★★ THE 8-BIT AND 16-BIT HALVES OF EVERY ARITHMETIC ROW, LANDED 2026-08-23 (cycle P29) TOGETHER WITH THE 2-BYTE IMMEDIATE SLOT THAT WAS BLOCKING THEM — [[D-ASM-X86-NO-16BIT-IMMEDIATE-SLOT]]. The previous cycle declared NONE of them rather than ship the family with a hole in one width: `addw $5, %ax` is `66 81 /0 iw`, and with no 2-byte immediate slot the only writable row would have emitted FOUR immediate bytes where the instruction takes two — a corrupt instruction stream with no diagnostic. With the slot in place the whole family lands at once, in the same four shapes the 32/64-bit rows already carry: register-direct, register-immediate, memory SOURCE and memory DESTINATION. ✔MEASURED per spelling against GNU as 2.42. ⚠ The BYTE forms carry `forceRexPrefix` on the TARGET side, and that is correctness rather than size: without a REX prefix, byte-register encodings 4..7 name the legacy high bytes ah/ch/dh/bh instead of spl/bpl/sil/dil.

⚠ `imulw` HAS NO `imulb` SIBLING, AND THAT IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN AN OMISSION: ✔GNU as 2.42 REJECTS `imulb %al, %cl` — x86 has no two-operand byte IMUL, only the one-operand AL form. Declaring one would accept input no reference assembler takes, which is the same defect as refusing input they do.

★ THE `l` HALVES OF `not`/`neg` LANDED 2026-08-23 ALONGSIDE THEIR MEMORY FORMS, and their absence was a plain hole rather than a decision: the target has declared width-32 `not`/`neg` variants since FC3 c2, GNU as 2.42 assembles `notl`/`negl`, and every other ALU spelling in this table already shipped as a q/l pair. Accepting input no reference assembler takes and refusing input they do accept are the same defect ([[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]], which is bidirectional).

★★★ `cmp` AGAINST MEMORY IS COMPLETE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS FROM 2026-08-23 (cycle P29) — [[D-ASM-X86-CMP-AGAINST-MEMORY-DIRECTION-IS-UNELECTABLE]] CLOSED. ⚠ THE ROW STILL NAMES ONE OPCODE, AND THAT IS THE POINT: the two directions are two VARIANTS of `cmp` separated by the target-side `guard.memoryDestination` axis, never two candidate opcodes here. A dialect that named the winner per shape would be a drifting second copy of the target's guard table — which `assembly_config.hpp` forbids by name — so the missing fact went onto the INSTRUCTION (`kLirInstFlagMemoryIsDestination`), where the text lowering AND the encoder both read it and cannot disagree. ✔MEASURED, GNU as 2.42: `cmpq %r14, 4096(%r15)` is `4d39b7…` and `cmpq 4096(%r15), %r14` is `4d3bb7…`; the two build the BYTE-IDENTICAL LIR operand list, so before the axis existed declaring either would have silently encoded the other for the opposite spelling.

★★★ THE WIDTH-EXTENDING MOVES — [[D-ASM-X86-WIDTH-EXTENDING-MOVES-UNSPELLABLE]] CLOSED 2026-08-23 (cycle P29). Each row states TWO widths: `width` is the SOURCE — the number that reaches the LIR instruction and elects the target's encoding variant — and `destWidth` the DESTINATION. ⚠ THE SECOND NUMBER IS NOT DECORATION: it is what lets the lowering check each register against its OWN role instead of requiring them all to agree, so `movzbl %cl, %ecx` is accepted while `movzbl %cl, %rcx` is refused. ✔Both answers MEASURED against GNU as 2.42, which accepts the first and rejects the second — the conformance runs BOTH ways. ★★ THE DESTINATION WIDTH PICKS THE OPCODE, not a guard: `movzbl` is `0F B6` and `movzbq` is `REX.W 0F B6`, two machine instructions, and one (opcode, operandKinds, width) triple cannot denote both — `validate()` refuses the second as unreachable. Hence `zext32`/`sext32`/`zext16`/`sext16` beside the existing `zext`/`sext`, exactly as `load_subreg` sits beside `load`. ⚠ `movsbl` vs `movsbq` is a VALUE difference and not a length one: for a negative byte the 32-bit destination yields 0x00000000FFFFFF80-shaped bits and the 64-bit one 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF80, so encoding either as the other is a wrong answer.

★ CONTROL FLOW — and the row where AT&T spells TWO instructions the same way. gas writes BOTH branches `jmp`: `jmp foo` is direct and `jmp *%rax` is indirect, distinguished only by the star on the operand (which is why `attIndirect` is a grammar rule and not decoration — dropping the star would silently turn an indirect jump into a direct one).
★★ SO THE ROW NAMES BOTH TARGET OPCODES, AND THE QUOTE THAT USED TO SIT HERE IS RETIRED RATHER THAN CARRIED. This row was `["jmp"]` under a comment quoting a MEASURED load-time refusal of the honest pair (`A0008 … one spelling cannot denote both … there would be nothing to elect over`). That measurement was true of the one-class-per-row engine and is FALSE of this one: election now spans terminator KINDS on a two-sided key — the DIALECT says whether the operand carried its indirect marker, the TARGET says which of its opcodes is `terminatorKind: indirect-br`. ✔RE-MEASURED 2026-08-13 with the pair in place, through the CLI on x86_64:pe64-x86_64-windows-exec: the document LOADS (no A0008 at load), `jmp foo` still lowers to `jmp` and links (rc=0), and `jmp *%rax` now elects `jmp_indirect`. A true measurement left standing after its subject changed is this tree's recurring defect, so the quote goes with the code it described.
⚠ `jmp *%rax` STILL DOES NOT BUILD, AND THE REASON MOVED WITH IT — it is now a DERIVABILITY refusal, not an opcode one. LIR records an indirect branch's address-taken successor blocks; no interior label of the function has a relocation bound against it, and a `.s` binds one only by materializing a label's address (`lea` of a label) or by listing labels in a jump table (`.quad <label>`), both still refused. The diagnostic names that missing INPUT, so the day interior-label relocation lands the same lowering succeeds and only the condition stops holding. Anchored: D-ASM-INDIRECT-BRANCH-SUCCESSOR-SET-UNSTATED (the successor half, blocked on D-ASM-INTERIOR-LABELS-NOT-ADDRESSABLE-AT-AN-OFFSET) · D-ASM-ATT-INDIRECT-BRANCH-INEXPRESSIBLE (the expressibility half, closed by this row).

★★ THE CONDITIONAL BRANCHES, each naming an EXISTING `TargetCondCode`. ⚠ THE SIGNED/UNSIGNED SPLIT IS THE PART THAT MISCOMPILES SILENTLY IF GUESSED: AT&T's `jl/jle/jg/jge` are SIGNED (`slt/sle/sgt/sge`) and its unsigned peers are spelled `jb/jbe/ja/jae` (`ult/ule/ugt/uge`) — a table built by matching letters would map `jbe` to `sle` and quietly reverse every unsigned comparison near the sign boundary. gas's `jz`/`jnz` are accepted ALIASES of `je`/`jne`, and per [[feedback_reference_compilers_are_the_spec]] an alias the reference assembler accepts is not optional. ⓘ The arm64 sibling spells this same set `b.eq`/`b.lt`/`b.lo`/… — different letters, identical `cond` values, which is what 'the condition vocabulary is target-shared and the spelling is dialect-owned' looks like in practice.

★★★ THE TWO ZERO-OPERAND SPELLINGS A REAL `__asm__` WRITES — and the reason they land now rather than with the rest of the arithmetic. Both target opcodes were declared in an earlier cycle and NEITHER had a producer: `opcodeByMnemonic` resolved them, the encoders were pinned by their measured bytes, and NO source language could reach either one, because C's front end has no spelling for them and this dialect had no row. An opcode with no producer is a capability that exists only in a table — the same 'never connected' shape the `mov`/W-form row above records, where the target grew a variant specifically so a `.s` could write `mov w0, w1` and the `.s` could not.
★★ `nop` IS THE ONE INSTRUCTION WHOSE ENTIRE PURPOSE IS TO OCCUPY BYTES, so it is also the one whose row proves the zero-operand path end to end: `asmStatement` mints NO tail child at all (its $comment calls that 'a real third case, not a degenerate one'), and until something in this table declared a zero-operand spelling the shipped dialects exercised that arm with `ret` alone — a TERMINATOR, which takes a different route through the lowering than a plain instruction does.
★★★ `rdtsc` IS THE ROW WITH THE REAL CLIENT: sqlite's own `src/hwtime.h` writes `__asm__ volatile("rdtsc" : "=a"(lo), "=d"(hi))` — the `"=a"`/`"=d"` constraints the target's `asmConstraints` block already binds. ✔MEASURED with gcc 13.3.0 (2026-08-14, source fed as base64 so no shell quoting could alter a byte): the BASIC form `__asm__("rdtsc")` emits `rdtsc` verbatim into the `#APP` block, which is exactly the text this row must read.
⚠ NEITHER ROW DECLARES A CONDITION AND NEITHER MAY: both target opcodes are `result: none` / `result: none` with no `condCodeFromPayload`, and `resolveRows` refuses a `cond` on an opcode that reads none — in both directions, once per dialect row, at config time rather than at the first `.s` line that uses it.
★ `width: 64` FOLLOWS THE `ret` PRECEDENT DIRECTLY ABOVE, and on a zero-operand spelling it is inert by construction rather than by luck: `effectiveWidth` reconciles a declared width against the width DERIVED from the register operands, and there are no register operands to derive one from. Both target opcodes declare a single width-ABSENT encoding variant (`guard.operandKinds: []`), which matches any width — so the key states the dialect's default and can never disagree with an operand that is not there.

directives.$comment: ★ A DIRECTIVE IS A VERB, NOT A STRING. The engine switches on the closed `verb` set; the SPELLING is this dialect's. gas's `.globl`/`.global` are two spellings of one verb, which is exactly the shape this table exists to express. An undeclared directive fails loud naming the spelling and this dialect — never ignored, because a silently-dropped `.globl` produces a binary whose entry symbol is local and whose link failure points nowhere near the cause.

★★★ `.type NAME, @function` — THE DIRECTIVE THAT SAYS WHICH LABELS ARE FUNCTIONS, AND WITHOUT IT THE COMPILER IS GUESSING. This row USED to be `ignoredAnnotation`, on the reasoning that DSS derives ELF symbol types from the LIR shape. That reasoning was true and the conclusion was still wrong: with every label minting a function, a `.s` with an intra-function branch target could not be expressed at all, and the operator's ruling on the corpus example that relied on the guess was *"an example that only works because the compiler guesses is the example being wrong."* The label→function question is decided HERE, by the file, and every label NOT so marked is a BLOCK in whatever function is open.
★ `marker` IS WHY `.type foo, @object` DOES NOT MINT A FUNCTION. Both are `.type`; only the operand distinguishes them, so the spelling alone cannot carry the verb and the engine must be told which operand text means 'function'. ⚠ AND THE MARKER IS PER-DIALECT, NOT PER-ENGINE: ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13, aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc writes `%function` where x86_64 gcc writes `@function` (see `asm-arm64-gas.lang.json`, whose row differs in exactly this one string). Hard-coding either spelling in the engine would have rejected half of the reference compilers' output.

★★★ THE DATA SURFACE, LANDED 2026-08-13 — AND THE ASYMMETRY IT CLOSES IS THE FINDING, NOT THE ROWS. Until now this dialect declared NO data-defining directive at all while its arm64 sibling declared the full family, so the identical engine verbs (`sectionData` / `emitData` / `reserveFillBytes`) were exercised by exactly ONE dialect. A mechanism witnessed by one signatory is the weaker claim this project keeps having to walk back; these rows make the second dialect a witness rather than a promise.
★★ `.section` IS THE OPERAND-TAKING FORM AND `.rodata` IS `operandOnly` — the same shape the arm64 document carries, and the same measurement backs it on THIS port: ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13, x86_64 `as` rejects a bare `.rodata` (`unknown pseudo-op`) and accepts `.section .rodata` (rc=0, PROGBITS+A). `.section` models the section NAME ONLY; a flags/type operand FAILS LOUD naming what it will not interpret, because those operands decide whether the section is writable/executable/zero-fill and this build derives all three from the section kind.
⚠ AND THE REFUSAL COMES FROM TWO DIFFERENT SITES, WHICH THIS BANNER USED TO ELIDE AND WHICH A READER WOULD OTHERWISE MEET AS A SURPRISE. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 through the real CLI, not recalled: `.section .rodata,@progbits` / `,1` / `,a` all reach the DIRECTIVE handler and get `A0008 — '.section' carries 2 operands; this build models the section NAME and nothing else`, which quotes the offending operand and states the rule. But the exact line gcc writes — `.section .rodata,"a",@progbits` — never gets there: this token table declares no string literal, so it dies at `P000E: got illegal character 0x22`. BOTH refuse (rc=1, no artifact, the flags are never applied and never ignored), so there is no silent path either way; only the QUALITY of the message differs. The day this dialect grows a string token (`.ascii`/`.asciz` need one) the quoted form starts lexing and MUST land on the operand-count refusal — which it will, because that guard counts operands rather than matching spellings. Pinned in `tests/asm/test_asm_shipped_dialects.cpp` from both ends.

★★★ THE ELEMENT WIDTHS ARE THIS DIALECT'S, AND `.word` IS EXACTLY WHY. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 rather than recalled — x86_64 `as` on a file with one label per directive, offsets read back with `objdump -t` (0x00, 0x01, 0x03, 0x05, 0x09, 0x11; each delta IS the width of the directive above it): `.byte`→1, `.word`→**2**, `.short`→2, `.long`→4, `.quad`→8. The arm64 sibling measured `.word`→**4** with the same instrument and the same binutils. One spelling, two widths, one build of the assembler — an engine that 'knew' a width for `.word` would silently halve or double every table on one of the two ports.
⚠ `.xword` IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT AND THAT IS ALSO MEASURED: x86_64 `as` REJECTS it (`unknown pseudo-op`) while aarch64 accepts it as 8 bytes. Declaring it here would accept what the reference assembler does not, which the bar forbids in the same breath as refusing what it does.
ⓘ `.hword` is likewise absent: x86_64 `as` ACCEPTS it (rc=0) but its width was not measured in this run, and a width guessed from the arm64 port is precisely the mistake the `.word` row exists to warn about. It stays undeclared and fails loud by name until somebody measures it.

★ THREE SPELLINGS, ONE VERB — the byte COUNT first, an OPTIONAL fill byte second. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13 on this port too: x86_64 `as` accepts BOTH `.space 4, 7` and `.zero 4, 7` rc=0, so `.zero` is not a fill-less special case and all three share the verb. See the arm64 sibling's row for the two deliberate divergences (an out-of-range fill is refused here where gas truncates-and-warns; a non-zero fill in a zero-fill section is warned-and-ignored exactly as gas does).

★★★ THE `.cfi_*` FAMILY — CALL FRAME INFORMATION, HONOURED AS OF 2026-08-17 (D-ASM-CFI-UNWIND-INFO-SILENTLY-DROPPED). ✔MEASURED 2026-08-13, `gcc -O1 -fno-ident -fcf-protection=none -S` on a five-line C function: SIX `.cfi_*` lines against FIVE instructions. Nothing else in a `.s` is so unavoidable — `-fasynchronous-unwind-tables` is ON by default on every Linux target.
★★★ WHAT CHANGED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE ROW SET: every one of these was `ignoredAnnotation` — parsed, accepted and DROPPED — so a `.s` assembled, ran correctly, and COULD NOT BE UNWOUND (no debugger backtrace, and an exception thrown through the frame terminating instead of propagating). They now bind the SHARED `CfiOpKind` vocabulary through the `frameRule` verb, and DSS emits real `.eh_frame` from them.
★★ THE `rule` NAMES A `CfiOpKind`, NOT A STRING THIS DOCUMENT INVENTS. The closed set lives in `core/types/cfi.hpp` and is shared with the C compiler's own frame producer and with every format's unwind writer; the SPELLING is this dialect's. That the two line up 1:1 here is not a coincidence — `cfi.hpp` states that every enumerator was written from a `.cfi_*` spelling a real assembler emits — but the binding is DECLARED, so a dialect spelling a rule differently needs no engine change.
⚠ THE OPERANDS ARE DWARF REGISTER *NUMBERS*, NOT REGISTER NAMES — `.cfi_offset 6, -16` means DWARF register 6 (`%rbp`), not the integer six, and DWARF 6 is HARDWARE 5. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17 on gcc 13.3.0 (x86_64 and aarch64): the compiler emits numbers EXCLUSIVELY, never a name. ✔MEASURED the same day on GNU as 2.42: `.cfi_offset 6, -16`, `.cfi_offset %rbp, -16` and `.cfi_offset rbp, -16` all assemble rc=0 and produce BYTE-IDENTICAL `DW_CFA_offset: r6 (rbp) at cfa-16`, so both forms are read here and resolved through the TARGET's `registers[].dwarfNumber` table — the same table the `.eh_frame` writer reads on the way out, which makes a round trip the identity.
★ WHICH SPELLINGS ARE HERE IS DECIDED BY WHAT THIS DIALECT CAN PARSE, NOT BY WHAT gas ACCEPTS, because a row whose operands cannot lex is a row that can never be reached. The three deliberately ABSENT ones all take a DOTTED SYMBOL operand this dialect cannot yet spell (`.cfi_personality 0x9b,DW.ref.__gxx_personality_v0`, `.cfi_lsda`, `.cfi_sections .debug_frame`); they stay fail-loud at the directive lookup, which names them. Anchored under D-ASM-ATT-GAS-SURFACE-INCOMPLETE.

★★ `.cfi_adjust_cfa_offset N` IS A DELTA ON THE ASSEMBLER'S RUNNING STATE, AND DWARF HAS NO OPCODE FOR IT. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17, GNU as 2.42: with the CFA offset at 48, `.cfi_adjust_cfa_offset 16` emits an ABSOLUTE `DW_CFA_def_cfa_offset: 64`; at the initial state `.cfi_adjust_cfa_offset 0` emits `DW_CFA_def_cfa_offset: 8`. So gas folds it against its own running state, and so does this producer — `dwarf_cfi.hpp` REFUSES an unresolved `adjust_cfa_offset` outright, naming the producer as the tier that must fold. The rule is still DECLARED as `adjust_cfa_offset` rather than as `def_cfa_offset`, because that is what the SOURCE says; the fold is the engine's.

★★★ `.cfi_rel_offset reg, off` IS `.cfi_offset reg, off − <current CFA offset>` — THE SAME RULE IN A DIFFERENT COORDINATE SYSTEM, WHICH IS WHY IT NAMES `offset` AND SETS A FLAG RATHER THAN GETTING A RULE OF ITS OWN. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17, GNU as 2.42: with the CFA offset at 48, `.cfi_rel_offset 6, 8` emits `DW_CFA_offset: r6 (rbp) at cfa-40` — 8 − 48 = −40, and there is no distinct DWARF opcode. A second `CfiOpKind` for it would put ONE fact in two places and make every consumer carry both arms forever.

★★ `.cfi_return_column N` — THE CHECK *IS* THE HONOURING. The column is a CIE-level fact and DSS derives it from the target's own `dwarfReturnAddressColumn` (16 on x86_64 — a synthetic column no register carries; 30 on aarch64). A file naming the SAME column is the no-op gcc emits; one naming a DIFFERENT column is asking for a per-function override a single shared CIE cannot express, and is REFUSED naming both numbers. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17: gas takes any value here (`.cfi_return_column 3` really does write `Return address column: 3`), so accepting it silently would let a `.s` redefine where the return address lives and have no effect whatever.

⛔⛔ `.cfi_signal_frame` IS DECLARED AND DELIBERATELY REFUSED, FOR A REASON THAT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN COSMETIC. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17, GNU as 2.42: it changes the CIE's AUGMENTATION STRING from 'zR' to 'zRS' — a CIE-level property, so a signal frame and an ordinary frame CANNOT SHARE A CIE (assembling this repo's corpus file produced TWO CIEs in one object for exactly that reason). DSS emits ONE shared CIE per module by construction and `dwarf_cfi.hpp` writes 'zR' unconditionally, so honouring the directive is not possible here and accepting it would drop the one fact it states — telling an unwinder NOT to back the return address up by one byte when looking up the caller. Refused by name until a per-CIE-augmentation writer exists.

⛔⛔ `.cfi_escape` IS DECLARED AND DELIBERATELY REFUSED, AND THE MEASUREMENT BELOW IS WHY — IT IS NOT CAUTION. It states RAW DWARF CFA BYTES that nothing can validate or re-encode for Win64 `UNWIND_INFO`, so accepting them would re-create D-ASM-CFI-UNWIND-INFO-SILENTLY-DROPPED's own defect INSIDE its fix. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-17, GNU as 2.42, on this repo's own corpus file as it then stood: `.cfi_escape 0x10, 0x06, 0x02` declares a 2-byte DWARF expression for register 6 and supplies ZERO expression bytes — so the reader consumes the NEXT TWO BYTES OF THE CFI PROGRAM as the expression body, and the following `.cfi_restore 6` VANISHES from the unwind program. `as` returns rc=0 with no diagnostic. gas emits the bytes verbatim and validates NOTHING; a build that accepted them would inherit exactly that.
